This week I did around 40 code reviews, about 8 a day. You can’t review at that pace while still writing code yourself without drastically lowering the quality of your reviews. One PR this week made me notice I’d stopped reviewing test files.

Unit tests are the base of the pyramid and the majority of our tests. Yet halfway through a big diff I tell myself, “those are just tests, I have enough files to get through.” I know they matter, but I skip them.

A lot of AI generated tests are useless, so this is a particularly bad time to skip them. I’d also forgotten that reading tests is how you understand what the code is supposed to do. If you skip them, you’re not really reviewing the PR.

It’s a bad habit I got into without noticing. I’m going back to opening test files first and giving them the same attention as the code they cover. They tell me what the code claims to do before I read how it does it. If that means fewer reviews per week, fewer is the honest number.

Do you skip test files too?

clarification.response:
The passage has a polished personal-post structure, but my earlier assessment gave some ordinary writing conventions too much weight as AI signals. Its more noticeable friction comes from a few compressed connections and shifts from personal experience to general claims. Those deserve separate treatment.

1. The narrative arc

The progression is clear: a PR exposes a habit, the review count explains the pressure, the third paragraph explains what gets lost, and the fourth commits to a change.

That is a normal structure for a professional reflection. It helps readers understand why the incident matters. An AI-like impression can arise when each paragraph performs its assigned role so neatly that the experience feels arranged around a predetermined lesson. There is a little of that here, particularly in the movement from admission to moral conclusion to commitment.

However, the structure itself creates no clarity problem. Making it less organised would not necessarily make it more personal. The relevant question is whether the connections feel earned; most of them do.

2. “They’re the base of the pyramid and make up the majority of our tests”

These two descriptions serve different purposes. “Base of the pyramid” invokes their place in a testing model; “majority of our tests” describes your team’s actual situation. Together, they emphasise how much you are overlooking.

The pyramid reference is an ordinary convention in writing for developers. My earlier suggestion that the audience probably does not need it was too categorical: a familiar concept can still provide useful emphasis.

Its slightly AI-like effect comes from pausing a personal account to supply textbook context. The sentence briefly sounds as though it is establishing the importance of unit tests for completeness. That effect overlaps with a relevance issue, rather than a factual or grammatical problem: the reader must connect the pyramid reference to why skipping these files matters. Keeping both substantive claims is possible; their relationship to your admission needs to carry the sentence.

3. “You haven’t really reviewed the PR if you haven’t read its tests”

In context, this turns your discovery into a standard for what counts as a review. “Really” does substantial work: it distinguishes completing a review action from doing the work you believe that action requires.

That is a conventional opinion-post move. A firm conclusion fits the subject and your candid voice. It can also sound AI-like because it packages the preceding explanation into a concise, portable lesson.

The more specific friction is the shift in scope. You begin with what you have been skipping, then state what counts as reviewing for anyone. The earlier “You can’t review at that pace…” makes the same move. These are broader claims, not merely descriptions of your week.

That does not make them unclear, but it changes the tone from reflection to instruction. If those general claims are intentional, preserving them means accepting some of that assertiveness. Turning everything into a personal qualification would change the substance, not just improve the style.

4. The closing question

“Do you ever get halfway through a diff and leave the test files unread?” returns to the exact situation in the opening. It invites readers to admit a recognisable behaviour rather than answer a vague question about review quality.

Closing with a question is an ordinary social-post convention. It can resemble an AI-generated engagement prompt, but this question is closely connected to the experience described. Its repetition also gives the passage a deliberate frame.

There is no significant clarity problem here. Whether it feels formulaic depends partly on the cumulative structure: after an orderly lesson and commitment, another familiar closing device can make the construction more visible. Removing it is an editorial preference, not a necessary repair.

5. The numbers and internal excuse

“Around 40 code reviews, about 8 a day” establishes the workload. The quoted thought—“those are just tests, I have enough files to get through”—shows how that workload affects an actual decision.

These details make the account concrete. They are not evidence of human authorship; generated writing can contain equally specific details. Their value is that they explain the behaviour rather than merely asserting that you were busy.

The internal excuse is especially effective because it exposes an unflattering piece of reasoning without explaining it away. I would preserve that voice.

6. “I’m skipping unit tests too”

My earlier explanation overstated the problem. This does not necessarily imply that unit tests are separate from test files. Readers can understand “too” as adding another troubling aspect of the admission.

Nevertheless, its reference is uncertain: what previously mentioned category are unit tests being added to? You have already said you skip test files generally. The intended emphasis appears to be that this includes the tests forming most of your suite.

That is a local clarity problem, with little specifically AI-like about it. It can be repaired at the level of the connective while preserving every substantive claim.

7. “A lot of AI generated tests are useless, which makes skipping test files even worse”

The intended connection is understandable: tests may be present without providing useful verification, so their presence makes careful review especially necessary.

But “which makes” compresses that reasoning. “Useless” also leaves the particular failure unspecified. The reader supplies the missing connection between weak generated tests and your responsibility to inspect them.

This is where clarity and an AI-like impression overlap most. Smooth causal transitions can make an argument sound complete before it has fully expressed its reasoning. Here, however, “useless” also contributes to your blunt voice.
